Need to search first.I've finished the notes, but they don't cover all three parts of your request. I hit the tool limit before I could open any full pages. Everything below comes from the search-result excerpts of each page. Those excerpts are often cut off, so some verses have thin or no notes, and points worth checking against the full page are marked.

**What's missing:**
- **Part 2 (differences between Protestant traditions):** I found nothing. None of the pages I saw show Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican teachers disagreeing on these verses. The interpretive disputes I found are between individual commentators, not traditions.
- **Part 3 (other views):** The Catholic and Orthodox sites, bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org weren't searched, and I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. The only partial exception is two Septuagint/Vulgate/Luther readings reported by Lange and Gill (v. 1 and v. 18).
- **Missing verses:** v. 5 is covered only by Gill. I found nothing specific on v. 21.

---

**v. 1**
- **Why Judah fell:** Guzik says Judah fell because it was unfaithful to God, not because of empires or politics. He also notes the writer skips straight over the 70 years of exile between v. 1 and v. 2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-9/
- **Which "Book of the Kings":** Gill says this means the kings' official annals and journals, not the biblical books of Kings. The northern tribes' family records were lost with their exile, which is why the list stops with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
- **Where the sentence breaks:** Gill says that, following the Hebrew accent marks, "Judah" starts a new sentence ("But Judah was carried away…"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
- **The older reading:** Lange notes that the Septuagint, the Latin Vulgate and Luther's Bible attach "Judah" to the previous phrase ("kings of Israel and Judah"). He considers that reading arbitrary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **Lessons on sin:** Matthew Henry says the exile should be remembered as a warning. When we speak of our own troubles, he says, we should admit they came "for my transgression." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_009.cfm
  - The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes put it as "sin means exile," because sin divides and separates. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **How reliable the lists are:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Israel kept public family registers from the start. They regard these lists as authoritative and protected from error by divine inspiration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/9-1.htm
- **Who wrote this line:** Clarke cites Rashi ("Jarchi"), who took this as Ezra's own words about a register he found in Babylon and copied into the earlier chapters. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/9-1.html

**v. 2**
- **When the "first inhabitants" lived (disputed):**
  - Gill: these are people who came back first under Cyrus and moved into their old properties. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
  - Clarke: they were the first to return, which implies others settled in Jerusalem later. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/9-2.html
  - Keil and Delitzsch disagree. They argue the phrase can only mean people who lived there *before* Judah went into exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/9-1.htm
  - The excerpt from the Ryrie-linked page on preceptaustin says plainly that 9:2-34 is about resettlement *after* the exile. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_chronicles_commentaries
- **Why "Israelites":** Guzik quotes Poole: using the old name "Israelites" shows the split between the two kingdoms has been wiped out and the people reunited. Guzik also quotes Trapp, who saw God's providence in keeping the land empty until its people came back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-9/
- **The four groups:** Gill sees four classes: ordinary people, priests, Levites who assisted the priests, and temple servants (Nethinim). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
  - Dummelow says "Israelites" means the laity, as opposed to the clergy. He calls 9:2-34 a "defective duplicate" of Nehemiah 11 with different names. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/1-chronicles-9.html
- **The temple servants:** Guzik quotes a writer who says the Hebrew word means "given ones." They may have been captives spared and made to serve the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-9/
  - The Pulpit Commentary says their work was fairly lowly, but God accepted it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **How this list relates to Ezra and Nehemiah:** A Bible Hub article suggests "the first to resettle" may sum up several waves of return. It says the Chronicler groups people by their role in worship. https://biblehub.com/q/why_do_returnee_lists_differ_in_1_chr,_ez,_neh.htm

**v. 3**
- **Northerners in Jerusalem:** Gill thinks the Ephraimites and Manassites had fled south. They either came when Jeroboam brought in idol worship or when Samaria fell, then went into exile with Judah and came back with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
- **Why "Israel":** On the parallel in Nehemiah 11, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the name "Israel" was used because many people from all the tribes had mixed together. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Neh/Neh_011.cfm

**v. 4**
- **Compared with Nehemiah:** Clarke says the list is nearly the same as those in Ezra and Nehemiah and records those who came first with Zerubbabel. He thinks Nehemiah's longer list probably includes later arrivals. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-9.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain the differences the same way: Chronicles lists the first group, Nehemiah later ones. They add that people's names were often changed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Neh/Neh_011.cfm

**v. 5**
- **"Shilonites":** Gill says this probably doesn't refer to the town of Shiloh. More likely it means the "Shelanites," descendants of Judah's son Shelah, and the Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) reads it that way. He identifies Asaiah with Maaseiah in Nehemiah 11:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**v. 6**
- **The 690:** Gill says this number covers all the descendants of Perez, Shelah and Zerah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**vv. 7–8**
- **Sallu's family line:** Gill says Nehemiah 11:7 gives it differently. Perhaps some men had two names. The others named are not mentioned anywhere else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**v. 9**
- **The 956:** Gill says the Benjamites in Jerusalem far outnumbered those from Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
- **Who the "heads" are:** Lange says "heads of families" refers to the named leaders from v. 4 on, not to the relatives being counted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **Lesson:** Matthew Henry says many people stayed behind in Babylon. Those whose spirits God stirred to return deserve to be remembered with honour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/9-1.html

**v. 10**
- **The three priests:** Gill says Jedaiah was the son of Jehoiarib. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**v. 11**
- **Who was "chief official" (disputed):**
  - Gill: Azariah is the same man as Seraiah. The title "ruler of God's house" belongs to Ahitub, not Azariah, since Joshua was high priest at the time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
  - Clarke disagrees. He says Azariah/Seraiah held the post, second only to high priest Jeshua, and probably guarded the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **Lesson:** The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes use the word "ruler" to teach that God's house is ordered by divine wisdom and that Christ alone is the true ruler of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html

**v. 12**
- **Names differ from Nehemiah:** Gill and the Pulpit Commentary both note that Nehemiah 11:12 adds three names between Jeroham and Pashhur. The Pulpit Commentary says Nehemiah's version of Maasai's line also differs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **Immer:** Gill says he headed one of the priestly divisions David set up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**v. 13**
- **"Able men":** Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: the Hebrew means "mighty men of valour," normally a military phrase. Guzik's point is that serving God takes a warrior's strength and courage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-9/
  - Gill says the priests needed physical strength and the courage to protect worship from corruption. He notes they outnumbered Judah and Benjamin together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary teaches that no ability is too good for God's service and that churches should spot and use gifted people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **The size of the clergy:** Clarke remarks on what a "prodigious number" of clergy served one temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-9.html

**v. 14**
- **Merari:** Gill notes that the list moves on to the Levites, the third class, and that Merari was Levi's third son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- **Jeduthun and Netophah:** Gill identifies Jeduthun with Ethan, one of David's singers. He places Netophah in Judah's territory and says it is unclear whether Elkanah or Berechiah lived there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm

**v. 17**
- **What gatekeepers did:** Gill says they guarded the gates of the tabernacle (the tent sanctuary). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
- **Four chiefs:** Lange says the four named men were captains of the four companies guarding the temple's four sides. He compares the "captains of the temple" in Luke 22:52. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **Compared with Nehemiah:** Ellicott compares Nehemiah 11:18-19. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/9-17.htm
- **Devotional reading:** Bible Hub's notes say the Korahites came from those spared by grace after Korah's rebellion. They call ordinary service important and see gatekeepers as pointing to Jesus as the Door (John 10). https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/9-17.htm

**v. 18**
- **The King's Gate:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say this was the king's private entrance from the palace into the temple. They think the old custom was kept even with no king, perhaps in hope that David's line would be restored. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/9-26.htm
- **"Camp of the Levites":** Gill links it to the Levites' camp around the tabernacle in the wilderness. He cites the Septuagint's rendering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
- **Order and faithfulness:** Guzik says the community wanted to arrange worship just as David had. He quotes F. B. Meyer on orderly worship where each person was faithful to his assigned task. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-9/

**v. 19**
- **Guarding the entrance:**
  - Gill: the gatekeepers kept impure people out. He calls the Levites the Lord's "host" or army and quotes Kimchi's view that they guarded the Most Holy Place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
  - Clarke cites Rashi: they let no one but priests approach during the service. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/9-19.html
  - Barnes (disputed) thinks this Shallum is a different person from the one in v. 17, with the separate job of guarding the inner doors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/9-19.html
- **Lowly but trusted work:** The Pulpit Commentary says this work looked lowly but was a position of trust, because only those with the right could enter the holy places. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html

**v. 20**
- **Who Phinehas was (disputed):**
  - Gill: the famous Phinehas, whom God helped against Zimri (Numbers 25). He cites the Targum's "the Word of the Lord was his help" and says the mention encouraged whoever held the post later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/9.htm
  - Matthew Henry, in a fragment that seems to be about v. 20, says this is "not the famous high priest of that name" but probably a well-known Levite. He reads the Targum's "Word of the Lord" as Christ, the eternal Word. Please check this on the full page. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_009.cfm
- **Encouragement for later gatekeepers:** Guzik quotes Selman: God being with Phinehas implies God was also with the gatekeepers of the Chronicler's day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-chronicles/1-chronicles-9.cfm
- **What "the Lord was with him" means:** The Pulpit Commentary says the phrase means more than God being present everywhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html

**v. 21**
- Guzik has a note that both Meshelemiah and Zechariah served under David. The excerpt breaks off partway through his explanation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-9/

**v. 22**
- **Samuel's role:**
  - Gill: Samuel drew up the plan and David carried it out. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-9.html
  - Barnes: the involvement of Samuel suggests David planned this while Saul was still alive. He also says the gatekeepers mostly lived in villages around Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/9-22.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary finds Samuel's involvement surprising, since no other Old Testament passage mentions it. It notes that the writer uses Samuel's old title "seer" and passes over Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-9.html
- **"Positions of trust":** Keil reads it as "on their fidelity," meaning they were appointed because they had proved faithful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/9-22.htm
- **When the 212 served (disputed):** Keil says the 212 can't come from David's time, because 1 Chronicles 26 counts only 93 gatekeepers then. Another note on the same page asks how a current count fits with the claim that David and Samuel appointed them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/9-22.htm
